_comment: Equivalence figures are standard pharmacology and stable. The prompts are the part you will want to tune — thresholds vary between guidelines and your trust will have its own policy. Each prompt fires on a declarative 'when' block evaluated against prednisolone-equivalent daily dose (peq), planned duration in weeks, dexamethasone daily dose (dex), and checkbox flags. No expressions are evaluated as code.

drugs.name: Dexamethasone
drugs.note: Long biological half-life and no mineralocorticoid effect — why it is preferred for cerebral oedema. Produces a greater glucose rise than prednisolone.

drugs.name: Methylprednisolone
drugs.note: Also produces a marked glucose rise.

drugs.name: Prednisolone
drugs.note: The reference drug for guideline dose thresholds.

drugs.name: Prednisone
drugs.note: Pro-drug of prednisolone; not marketed in the UK.

drugs.name: Hydrocortisone
drugs.note: Physiological replacement is roughly 15-25 mg/day in divided doses.

physiological.note: Below roughly hydrocortisone 15-25 mg/day equivalent (about dexamethasone 0.5-0.75 mg/day), you are at or under physiological replacement. Further reduction risks unmasking adrenal insufficiency rather than treating the original indication.

tabletStrengths.note: UK dexamethasone tablets are commonly 0.5 mg and 2 mg; 4 mg and 8 mg are also available. Doses below are rounded to achievable 0.5 mg multiples.

prompts.title: PJP prophylaxis indicated
prompts.text: Planned exposure crosses the widely used threshold of ≥20 mg prednisolone-equivalent daily for ≥4 weeks. Co-trimoxazole is first line. Check FBC at initiation and monthly. Consider stopping prophylaxis once the dose falls below 20 mg prednisolone-equivalent, and continuing longer if the patient is lymphopenic or on other immunosuppression.
prompts.source: NCCN 2024; JAMA Insights 2023. Thresholds differ between guidelines — see the alternative below.

prompts.title: PJP prophylaxis — consider on duration
prompts.text: Moderate-dose steroid continued for ≥8 weeks. ASH guidance suggests considering prophylaxis at ≥15 to <30 mg prednisolone-equivalent given for ≥8 weeks, continuous or intermittent, even though the ≥20 mg / 4-week rule may not be met.

prompts.title: PJP prophylaxis during concurrent chemoradiotherapy
prompts.text: Concurrent temozolomide and radiotherapy causes CD4 lymphopenia independent of steroid dose. PJP prophylaxis is conventionally given throughout the concurrent phase and continued until lymphocyte recovery, irrespective of whether the steroid threshold is met. Monitor lymphocyte count.
prompts.source: Stupp regimen; confirm against your local neuro-oncology protocol.

prompts.title: Baseline glucose before starting
prompts.text: Check HbA1c or fasting glucose before or at the start of treatment. Steroid-induced diabetes can develop in people with no prior glucose abnormality and is frequently missed without proactive monitoring.

prompts.title: Capillary glucose monitoring
prompts.text: Outpatients: capillary glucose at least once daily, timed 1-2 hours after the main meal or before the evening meal — this catches the characteristic afternoon and evening peak that follows morning steroid. Inpatients: four times daily. Act if glucose exceeds 12 mmol/L on two occasions within 24 hours. Usual target 6-10 mmol/L, with 6-12 acceptable, and looser targets in frailty, dementia, recent brain injury or end-of-life care.
prompts.source: JBDS-IP Management of Hyperglycaemia and Steroid Therapy

prompts.title: If hyperglycaemia develops
prompts.text: Dexamethasone and methylprednisolone raise glucose more than prednisolone or hydrocortisone, reflecting potency and half-life. Management is glucose-led rather than HbA1c-led during treatment. Involve the diabetes team early if the patient already has diabetes, and remember that glycaemic requirements fall as the steroid is tapered — insulin and sulfonylurea doses need reducing in step, or the patient will become hypoglycaemic.

prompts.title: Adrenal suppression — steroid card and sick day rules
prompts.text: More than about three weeks of supraphysiological steroid suppresses the HPA axis. Issue a steroid emergency card, counsel on sick day rules, and do not stop abruptly. Symptoms of adrenal insufficiency during tapering — fatigue, nausea, dizziness, myalgia — are easily mistaken for disease progression or steroid withdrawal and warrant a paused taper rather than a faster one.
prompts.source: MHRA steroid emergency card; Society for Endocrinology

prompts.title: Rebound cerebral oedema
prompts.text: Recurrence of headache, nausea or focal deficit during a taper may represent rebound oedema rather than tumour progression. Step back up to the last tolerated dose and taper more slowly rather than restarting at the original dose.

prompts.title: Dose timing
prompts.text: Give the last dose no later than early afternoon — around 2pm — to limit insomnia. Twice daily dosing at breakfast and lunchtime is usual for dexamethasone in cerebral oedema. Take with food.

prompts.title: Gastroprotection
prompts.text: Routine PPI cover for steroid alone is not well supported. Prescribe gastroprotection where there is concurrent NSAID or anticoagulant use, previous ulcer disease, or other risk factors.

prompts.title: Bone protection
prompts.text: Steroid exposure expected to last three months or more. Assess fracture risk and consider calcium, vitamin D and bisphosphonate per local guidance, particularly in older patients and those with prior fragility fracture.

prompts.title: Proximal myopathy
prompts.text: Steroid myopathy is common at higher doses and presents as difficulty rising from a chair or climbing stairs. It is a reason to taper, not to increase. Early physiotherapy referral helps.

prompts.title: Check the injection strength
prompts.text: UK dexamethasone injection is labelled as dexamethasone base (3.3 mg/mL) whereas older products and much of the literature express dexamethasone phosphate (4 mg/mL). Confirm which is meant when converting between oral and parenteral routes.
prompts.source: MHRA labelling guidance — verify current product literature.
